title: Before the Car: Hooves, Sails and Daydreams
summary: Long ago, if you wanted to go somewhere, you walked, rode a horse or bumped along in a cart pulled by animals. Clever people dreamed of carts that could move all by themselves, powered by springs, wind or even steam. But one big piece was still missing: a small, strong engine.

sections.heading: The Greatest Round Idea
paragraphs: Close your eyes and imagine a world without a single engine. No cars, no buses, no trains, no bicycles even. If you wanted to visit a town 50 kilometres away, you had three choices: walk for two days, ride an animal, or sit in a creaking cart while an ox plodded along at the speed of a slow stroll. For almost all of human history, that was simply how life worked.

Every car you have ever seen rolls on wheels, so our story starts with the wheel itself. Surprisingly, the wheel is much younger than farming or pottery. People had been growing crops for thousands of years before anyone put a round disc on an axle and used it to carry loads.

The oldest clues all appear at about the same time, roughly 3500 BCE, scattered across a wide area. In the city of Uruk, in Mesopotamia (the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in today's Iraq), scribes pressed little pictures of wheeled wagons into clay tablets dated to about 3500 to 3350 BCE. In southern Poland, archaeologists found a clay pot from about the same period, now called the Bronocice pot, scratched with what looks like a simple four-wheeled wagon. In northern Germany there are tracks of wheels from around 3400 BCE.

The oldest actual wooden wheel ever found was pulled out of a peat bog near Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia. It was made of ash planks, together with an oak axle, and tree-ring and radiocarbon dating puts it somewhere around 3340 to 3030 BCE. It survived more than 5,000 years because the wet, airless mud stopped it from rotting.

Those first wheels were solid: heavy discs made of planks fastened together. They were strong but clumsy. Around 2000 BCE, people on the grassy plains east of the Ural Mountains, in what archaeologists call the Sintashta culture, began making wheels with spokes. A spoked wheel is much lighter, and a light wheel can turn fast. Hitch two fast horses to a light cart with spoked wheels and you have a chariot, the speedy war-machine of the ancient world, which spread from Egypt to China.

Here is the important thing to notice. The wheel made carrying things much easier, because rolling is far less effort than dragging. But the wheel does not move by itself. Every wagon, cart and chariot still needed a muscle-powered animal or person in front of it. For the next five thousand years, the speed and range of land travel was limited by how fast, how far and how long an ox, a donkey, a mule or a horse could keep going.

sections.heading: Roads Built for Legions
paragraphs: Wheels are only as good as the ground under them. A cart on soft mud sinks; a cart on a rocky track shakes itself to pieces. The ancient people who understood this best were the Romans.

In 312 BCE a Roman official named Appius Claudius Caecus started building a military road heading south from Rome. It became the Via Appia, the Appian Way, and it was later stretched all the way to Brindisi on the heel of Italy, about 540 kilometres from Rome. The poet Statius called it the 'queen of roads'. Parts of it still exist today, lined with ancient tombs, and some stretches near Rome are still used by cars. In 2024 UNESCO added it to its World Heritage List.

The Romans built roads mainly for their armies. A legion could march quickly along a straight, firm road to wherever trouble broke out, and supply wagons could follow. Trade travelled the same routes: grain, wine, olive oil, pottery, letters and news. Over the centuries the empire built a gigantic network. Historians estimate that the total of all Roman roads was more than 400,000 kilometres, and that the main paved highways added up to roughly 80,000 kilometres, enough to wrap around the Earth twice.

A good Roman road was a layer cake. Workers dug a trench down to firm ground, then filled it with packed rubble and stones, then layers of coarse and fine concrete-like material, and finally a top surface of tightly fitted paving stones. The surface was curved, higher in the middle, so rain ran off into ditches on each side. The Greek historian Procopius later wrote that the stones of the Appian Way fitted so well that they seemed to have grown together.

Along the roads stood milestones, stone columns about one and a half metres tall. A Roman mile was a thousand paces, about 1,480 metres, which is where our word 'mile' comes from. The government also ran a messenger system with relay stations where tired horses could be swapped for fresh ones. Using these relays, a message could cover about 80 kilometres in a day, and the future emperor Tiberius is said to have once raced about 296 kilometres in 24 hours. Ordinary horse-drawn carts were much slower, managing about 40 to 50 kilometres in a day.

When the Western Roman Empire broke apart in the 400s CE, no central government was left to repair the network. Stones were taken away for building, drains clogged, and grass and mud slowly swallowed many routes. For more than a thousand years, most roads in Europe were little better than dirt tracks: dusty in summer, deep mud in winter, and full of ruts and potholes all year. In England, local parishes were supposed to keep their own roads in order, but they rarely had the money or the will to fix busy routes used by strangers.

Things only began to improve in the late 1600s and 1700s. In 1663 the English Parliament allowed tolls to be collected on part of the Great North Road to pay for repairs, and from this grew the 'turnpike trusts', groups that charged travellers at gates (the turnpikes) and used the money to maintain the road. By the 1830s about 1,000 trusts looked after roughly 30,000 miles (48,000 kilometres) of road in England and Wales, with nearly 8,000 toll gates. Engineers such as John Metcalf, Thomas Telford and John Loudon McAdam showed how to build dry, firm road surfaces again. You will meet McAdam properly in a later part of this story.

sections.heading: Life at the Speed of a Horse
paragraphs: For the people of the 1600s and 1700s, the fastest way across the land was the horse. A horse walking with a rider moves at about the same speed as a brisk human walker, around 6 kilometres per hour. It can trot or gallop much faster, but only for a short time before it gets tired. A rider who wanted to travel far in one day had to pace the animal carefully, or swap horses along the way.

That is how the stagecoach worked. A stagecoach was a big covered carriage that carried paying passengers on a regular timetable, pulled by a team of usually four horses. The trip was split into 'stages'. At the end of each stage, at an inn or post station, grooms quickly unhitched the sweaty, tired team and hitched up fresh horses. In Britain the first recorded stagecoach service ran from Edinburgh to the nearby port of Leith in 1610, and by the late 1600s coaches ran along England's main roads.

Early coaches were painfully slow by our standards. Until the late 1700s they averaged roughly 5 miles per hour (about 8 kilometres per hour), covering perhaps 60 to 70 miles in a long day. In 1754 a 'Flying Coach' from Manchester to London proudly advertised that it would arrive in four and a half days. Better roads and better coaches made a big difference: the journey from Cambridge to London fell from about two days around 1750 to under seven hours by 1820.

In 1784 a theatre owner named John Palmer persuaded the British government to try carrying the mail by fast coach instead of by riders on horseback. His test coach left Bristol at four in the afternoon on 2 August 1784 and reached London about 16 hours later, while the old post had sometimes taken up to 38 hours. Within about 13 years, mail coaches were running on 42 routes.

Inside, passengers were often squeezed shoulder to shoulder on hard seats, bounced by every rut, frozen in winter and choked with dust in summer. The cheapest tickets were for seats on the roof, out in the wind and rain. Highway robbers sometimes held up coaches on lonely stretches of road, and coaches could overturn on steep or icy hills.

Horses also had to be fed, housed and cared for, and that cost a fortune. A large horse eats roughly 10 kilograms of hay and grain every day and drinks dozens of litres of water. It needs a stable, a groom, a blacksmith for its shoes, and rest. To keep a single busy coach route running, a company needed a whole army of horses waiting at the inns along the way. One route between London and Newcastle, about 278 miles long, needed around 250 horses. A horse working hard pulling coaches might only last a few years before it was worn out.

And then there was the mess. Every town with lots of horses also had lots of manure, flies and smell. Street sweepers worked hard to clear crossings so that people could walk across without ruining their shoes. You will hear much more about horse-filled cities later in this story, but for now just picture a busy market street around 1750: carts, coaches, riders and pack animals all crowded together, and the ground underfoot not exactly clean.

So people had wheels, and in some places they had decent roads. What they did not have was a way to make a vehicle move without an animal pulling it. Some very clever people had been daydreaming about exactly that.

sections.heading: Leonardo's Clockwork Cart
paragraphs: Imagine leafing through the private notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian painter of the Mona Lisa, who was also an engineer, an inventor and a non-stop sketcher of ideas. Among drawings of flying machines, war machines and water pumps, there is a page that has puzzled and delighted engineers for a long time. It shows a squat, square wooden cart with three wheels and a jumble of gears and springs. It is now kept in a huge collection of his papers called the Codex Atlanticus, as sheet 812 recto, and scholars usually date it to around 1478, when Leonardo was in his mid-twenties and working in Florence.

For centuries nobody quite understood the drawing. Then, in the late twentieth century, researchers studying the sheet realised that it showed a self-propelled cart: a vehicle meant to move on its own without being pushed or pulled. The power came from big coiled springs, like the spring in a wind-up toy or an old clock, housed inside drum-shaped cases. You would wind the springs up tightly; as they slowly unwound, they turned the gears that drove the wheels.

Leonardo also seems to have solved some clever problems. A spring pushes hard when it is tightly wound and weakly when it is nearly unwound, which would make the cart jerk forward and then crawl. The design includes a balance wheel, the kind of regulator used in clocks, to keep the motion steady. There also appears to be a mechanism that could be set in advance so the cart would follow a planned route, turning at certain moments. In a way, it was a tiny programmable robot, more than 500 years old.

What was it for? It certainly was not a family car. It was far too small to carry a driver and would have run for only a short distance on each winding. Many historians think it was meant as a marvel for a festival or a theatrical show, where a cart that rolled across the stage by itself would make the audience gasp. Rich Italian rulers of the time loved such wonders.

It is very important to be clear about one thing: Leonardo did not build a car. As far as we know, the cart existed only on paper. But modern engineers have built working models from his drawing. A team in Florence is reported to have built one in 2004 that rolled along by itself, and a replica stands at Clos Lucé, the manor house in Amboise, France, where Leonardo spent his last years. These models show his idea could work, but they also show its limits. A spring can only store a small amount of energy. Once it runs down, someone has to wind it up again by hand. No spring could ever carry a family from one town to another.

sections.heading: Sailing on Sand: Simon Stevin's Wind Chariot
paragraphs: If springs were too weak, what about the wind? The wind pushes sailing ships across whole oceans, and it is completely free. In the summer of 1600, a brilliant Flemish-Dutch engineer named Simon Stevin decided to put a sail on wheels.

Stevin was one of the great thinkers of his age. In 1585 he wrote a little booklet called De Thiende ('The Tenth') that taught ordinary people to calculate with decimal fractions instead of awkward ones like three-sevenths, which helped make decimals popular in Europe. He studied how water pushes on dams and how weights balance on slopes, and he worked as an engineer and teacher for Prince Maurice of Orange, the military leader of the young Dutch Republic.

For Prince Maurice, Stevin built a 'sailing chariot', in Dutch a zeilwagen. Picture a wooden wagon a bit like a small boat on four wheels, with a mast and sails, and a rudder-like steering arrangement. Its playground was the wide, flat, firm sand of the Dutch coast at low tide, between the fishing village of Scheveningen, near The Hague, and the village of Petten further north.

According to the accounts of the time, on a test run around 1600 the chariot carried Stevin, Prince Maurice and about two dozen other passengers, some 28 people in all, racing along the beach faster than horses could run. Prince Maurice used it to entertain and impress important guests. Stories of the journey spread across Europe, and artists made engravings of the sail-powered wagon skimming along the shore. Stevin may even have been inspired by travellers' reports from China: in 1585 a Spanish writer described Chinese carts fitted with sails, and Chinese writings mention wind-driven carriages centuries earlier.

The original sailing chariot was lost long ago, though a model of it was kept at Scheveningen until 1802. Today, people still race 'land yachts' on wide beaches and dry lake beds, and they are the direct descendants of Stevin's idea.

But think about the problem. A sailing chariot only works where the ground is flat, wide and smooth, and only when the wind is blowing the right way. On a narrow, muddy, winding road between hedges, on a calm day, or with the wind in your face, it would go nowhere. The wind is free, but you cannot control it, so it was never going to replace the horse.

sections.heading: A Steam Toy for an Emperor
paragraphs: Now travel more than 7,000 kilometres east, to Beijing in the 1670s, to the court of the Kangxi Emperor of China, one of the longest-reigning and most curious rulers in Chinese history. Among his advisers was a European priest called Ferdinand Verbiest, known in China as Nan Huairen.

Verbiest was born in 1623 in Pittem, a village in Flanders (in today's Belgium). He became a Jesuit, a member of a Catholic religious order famous for its schools and scholars, and sailed to China, arriving in 1658. The Jesuits in Beijing were respected for their skill in astronomy and mathematics, because predicting eclipses and making accurate calendars mattered a great deal to the imperial government.

Verbiest's life was not always easy. In the 1660s he and other Jesuits were thrown into prison after their enemies at court accused them. But in 1669 he won a public contest in astronomy, predicting the length of shadows, the positions of the planets and an eclipse more accurately than his rival. The emperor put him in charge of the Imperial Observatory. Verbiest rebuilt it in 1673 with six large bronze instruments for measuring the sky, some of which you can still see on the old observatory platform in Beijing today. He also taught the young emperor geometry and even cast 132 cannons for the imperial army.

Around 1672, according to Verbiest's own writings, he designed a little self-moving cart as a toy to amuse the emperor. It was about 65 centimetres long, roughly the size of a large toy truck, far too small to carry a person or any cargo. On it sat a round metal container of water, heated by burning coals underneath. When the water boiled, steam rushed out of a narrow pipe and blew against a small wheel with blades, rather like wind blowing on a pinwheel. That bladed wheel was geared to the cart's wheels, so as it spun, the cart rolled forward. A tiller allowed it to be steered, and it is said it could run for over an hour.

Verbiest described this machine in a book called Astronomia Europaea ('European Astronomy'), finished in 1681 and printed in Germany in 1687, the year before he died after a fall from a horse. Because of that description, his little cart is often called the earliest known design for a steam-powered vehicle. Still, we have to be careful. No original drawing of it survives, and we only know about it from his writing, so historians cannot be completely sure exactly how it looked or how well it worked. And it was a toy, not a car: it never carried anyone anywhere.

Interestingly, it suggested a real idea. In 2021, students in Ingolstadt, Germany, built a replica based on Verbiest's description, and it worked well enough to show that his concept was possible. The power of boiling water, which people had played with since ancient Greek inventors spun little steam toys, could actually push a vehicle along.

sections.heading: The Missing Piece
paragraphs: Let us line up our three daydreams side by side. Leonardo's spring cart could move by itself, but its spring stored so little energy that it could only creep a short way. Stevin's sailing chariot could carry a crowd at amazing speed, but only on a wide beach with the right wind. Verbiest's steam cart used a fuel that could be carried along, but the tiny jet of steam could only push a toy.

Each inventor had found part of the answer. What none of them had was an engine: a machine small enough to fit on a vehicle, strong enough to move people and cargo, and able to keep running for hours on fuel that you carry with you. Horses were, in a sense, the best 'engines' anyone had. A horse turns hay into pulling power, can climb hills, steer around holes and keep going all day, and it even makes more horses.

In the early 1700s, real steam engines did finally appear in Britain. In 1712 an ironmonger named Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine to pump water out of coal mines. But Newcomen's engines were gigantic. Each filled a building several storeys high, ran slowly, and burned huge amounts of coal. Nobody could put a machine like that on wheels and drive it down a road.

Engineers kept improving steam engines through the 1700s, making them stronger and more efficient. And slowly a bold question began to form in the minds of a few people. If a steam engine could pump water and turn the machines of a factory, could a smaller, tougher one be made to move itself along the ground?

The first person to answer that question with a real, full-size machine was not a toy-maker, a showman or an emperor's astronomer. He was a soldier-engineer in the French army. He had a very practical and very heavy problem to solve: how to drag enormous bronze cannons into position without needing teams of horses. His answer would be a giant, clanking, puffing steam wagon, the first self-moving vehicle big enough to carry real loads, and it is waiting for us in the next part.

deepDive: Where and when was the wheel invented? The honest answer is that historians are not sure, and the debate is lively. Evidence for wheeled vehicles appears almost at the same moment, around 3500 to 3300 BCE, in places thousands of kilometres apart: pictographs from Uruk in Mesopotamia, the Bronocice pot in Poland, wheel ruts in northern Germany, clay model wagons in the steppes north of the Black Sea, and the Ljubljana Marshes wheel in Slovenia. Some archaeologists think the idea was invented once and spread very quickly along trade routes; others suspect separate inventions. Interestingly, the potter's wheel is even older in some places: one from the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture of Ukraine dates to the middle of the fifth millennium BCE. A key insight is that the hard part was not the round wheel but the precise fit between wheel and axle. If the hole in the wheel is too tight, it jams; too loose, it wobbles and wears out. That needed good tools and careful carpentry. Roman road numbers also need care. Figures such as '80,000 km of paved road' and '400,000 km in total' come from ancient lists, inscriptions and modern mapping projects, and they depend on what you count as a 'road'. Similarly, the stories of Stevin's sailing chariot come from accounts written by admirers, and modern writers repeat differing figures for its speed and distance, so it is wise to say only that it was reported to be faster than horses. Leonardo's cart is another case where interpretation matters. The drawing on Codex Atlanticus folio 812r was long thought to show something else; only careful study in the late twentieth century suggested it was a spring-driven, pre-programmable cart. Working models built since then are modern reconstructions, so they include some guesses about missing details. Finally, Verbiest's steam cart is known only from his own text. It used something like a steam turbine, steam blowing on a bladed wheel, rather than a piston engine. That is a reminder that turbines and piston engines are two quite different ways of turning steam into motion, and it was the piston engine that would power the first full-size vehicles.
funFact: The oldest wooden wheel ever found, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, is more than 5,000 years old and survived because it was buried in wet, airless mud.

check.q: Why couldn't Leonardo da Vinci's self-propelled cart have become a real family car?
check.a: Its springs stored only a little energy, so it could only go a short way before someone had to wind it up again (and it was only a design on paper)
wrong: It was powered by a steam boiler that kept exploding
It needed a team of four horses to start it
It could only move when the wind was blowing
